analysis.one_liner: Caps what patients can be charged for out-of-network emergency and hospital care, ending surprise medical bills.
analysis.headline: The bill won approval from a House health subcommittee by voice vote in July 2019 but never received a vote in the full committee or on the floor before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When you go to an emergency room or an in-network hospital, you can be treated by a doctor who has no contract with your insurance plan, and that doctor can bill you for the difference between the insured rate and their full charge — a 'surprise bill.' This bill stops that: patients would owe only their normal in-network copay, insurers would pay the out-of-network provider at a benchmark rate based on the median of negotiated rates, and doctors who are not hospital-based could still bill extra only if the patient signs a clear notice-and-consent form at least 72 hours in advance. It also requires insurers to keep accurate provider directories and funds state all-payer claims databases.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with private health insurance who gets emergency care or treatment at a hospital, since they would no longer owe surprise out-of-network charges beyond their normal copay. Insurers also gain predictability because they would pay providers a benchmark rate rather than contested charges.

how_it_helps.text: Caps patient cost-sharing for out-of-network emergency services at no more than what they would pay an in-network provider, counted toward the in-network deductible and out-of-pocket maximum.
Prohibits out-of-network emergency departments and doctors from balance billing patients for the difference between billed charges and the insurer's payment.

Extends the same protection to non-emergency care from out-of-network providers at in-network hospitals, labs, imaging centers, and ambulatory surgery centers, and bars facility-based providers like anesthesiologists, radiologists, and emergency physicians from balance billing even with notice and consent.
Requires insurers to verify and update provider directories at least every 90 days, remove unverified providers, and answer network-status questions within one business day.
Authorizes $50 million in grants for states to build all-payer claims databases and requires a Labor Department study of the bill's effects on premiums, out-of-pocket costs, and network adequacy.

analysis.who_pays: Out-of-network emergency physicians, physician staffing companies, and other providers lose the ability to collect balance bills from patients; insurers pay the claims, and providers argue the insurer-set benchmark would underpay them.

drawbacks.text: The payment benchmark is the median of the insurer's own negotiated rates, which leaves insurers largely in control of what providers get paid; the bill only adds an audit process for how insurers calculate it.

Non-facility-based out-of-network providers can still balance bill if a patient signs a written notice and consent at least 72 hours before service, a carve-out that critics could pressure patients into using.
The bill does not require plans to have adequate networks, so patients can still end up with out-of-network doctors; it only commissions a study of network adequacy.

Emergency air ambulance operators face only a new itemized-billing requirement and penalties for not itemizing, not a cap on what patients can be charged, even though air ambulance balance bills are among the largest patients receive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the benefit is substantial and concrete: the largest sources of surprise bills — emergency rooms and out-of-network specialists at in-network hospitals — would be closed off, with a narrow consent exception. The main cost falls on providers who built a business model around out-of-network billing, and the benchmark design tilts toward insurers because they set the median rate. Those tradeoffs were the reason provider groups fought the approach, but the patient-side protection itself is strong.

outcome.mechanism: After winning approval from the Health Subcommittee by voice vote in July 2019, the bill sat in the full Energy and Commerce Committee and never got a markup or floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representatives Frank Pallone, the Democratic chairman of the Energy and Commerce Committee, and Greg Walden, the committee's top Republican, introduced the bill together on July 9, 2019.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor Committees, and a subcommittee hearing on surprise billing was held before it was formally introduced.
On July 11, 2019, the Health Subcommittee considered and marked up the bill and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote.
No further action was taken — no full committee vote, no floor vote — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Providers whose revenue depends on out-of-network balance billing — including private-equity-backed emergency physician staffing firms — kept the practice intact for another year, while patients continued receiving surprise bills. Insurers also avoided the administrative burden of the bill's audit and directory requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Providers who bill patients surprise amounts

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee

for.name: Greg Walden
for.role: Ranking Member, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill alongside Chairman Pallone, giving it bipartisan leadership backing.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings before introduction, marked the bill up, and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote.

against.name: Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a full committee markup or vote after the subcommittee forwarded the bill in July 2019.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Advanced a rival surprise-billing bill in his committee that relied on arbitration between insurers and providers rather than a set payment benchmark, splitting House Democrats over the approach and stalling the Energy and Commerce version.

against.name: American Medical Association
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against fixing payments at a benchmark rate, arguing it would let insurers dictate below-market reimbursements to doctors.

against.name: Private-equity-backed emergency physician staffing firms
against.what_they_did: Ran a major campaign against benchmark-rate surprise-billing legislation, which threatened their business of billing patients the difference on out-of-network emergency care.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors were the Democratic chairman and the top Republican on the Energy and Commerce Committee, and it cleared subcommittee by voice vote; the resistance that stalled it came from within the majority's own committee rivalry and provider lobbying rather than a party-line vote, since it never reached one.

industries.note: These firms depend on billing patients the balance on out-of-network emergency care. The bill converts that revenue into a fixed insurer payment and categorically bars facility-based emergency physicians from balance billing, so their interest runs directly against the patient protection.

Insurers would pay out-of-network claims at a benchmark set from the median of their own negotiated rates, replacing providers' inflated charges, and their role as the rate-setters for out-of-network care would be locked in by law. Patients gain protection, but the mechanism routes the payment decision through the insurers.

Hospital emergency departments lose the ability to balance bill patients, but the hospital itself is paid a recognized amount by the insurer. Hospitals that host out-of-network specialists lose revenue while their patients gain protection.

Operators face only an itemized-billing requirement with penalties up to $10,000 per violation, not a cap on patient charges, even though air ambulance balance bills are among the largest surprise bills patients receive.
